title: Market Stall Pitch
goal: Your kid picks something to sell, figures out why someone would want it, writes a short pitch and sells it to real people at a stall. Family is fine for a first try; a real yard or market stall is even better. They learn to talk to strangers, handle a 'no,' and adjust on the fly.
need: Something to sell: homemade (lemonade, cookies, crafts), something they own (books, toys) or a service (dog walking, garden help)
A table, paper and markers for a sign and price tags
Customers: family, friends or neighbours (play money works for a practice round)

lesson.text: A pitch isn't a list of facts. In under 30 seconds it grabs attention, says what's in it for the buyer, and asks for the sale.
lesson.before: Hi. This is lemonade. It's one dollar.

model.line: Ice-cold lemonade to cool you right down, squeezed this morning.
Just one dollar, or two cups for $1.50.
Want to try a sip first?

lesson.modelNote: Naming the product gives a passer-by no reason to stop. Start with them (it's hot), say what they get (cooled down), then ask.

howTo.intro: Your hardest job comes before the stall: rounding up customers who aren't you. Pick a day when people will be around (a weekend, a family visit, a garage sale), and play a tough customer in practice so the actual ones feel easy.

plan.what: 'Sell me this', choose the product, set the price (Steps 1 and 2). Make the product if it's homemade.
Write the pitch and practise it (Step 3). 20 minutes.
Set up the stall, sell, then count it up (Steps 4 and 5).

troubleshoot.q: Your kid freezes with real customers
troubleshoot.a: Start with family only, then one neighbour. A small card with their first line on it helps.
That's real feedback. Try a different opening, a lower price or a free sample, and see what changes.
A table at your door on a busy afternoon, a garage sale, or a service door to door with you. Check local rules before selling homemade food.

fromHome.text: My daughter made two flavours of popcorn herself, bagged it, came up with her logo and her price, and set up her stand: 'Mais moi ça!', $2 a bag. She made $86. At her lemonade stand, she didn't wait behind the table. She walked out to strangers on the street and told them to come have a tasty, fresh lemonade.

skills.name: Persuasive speaking
skills.text: convincing someone it's worth their money

skills.name: Money sense
skills.text: pricing, value and what customers want

steps.title: Play 'sell me this'
steps.why: Selling a spoon to each other shows what a pitch is before your kid picks a product.
steps.kid: Grab any object in the room (a spoon, a sock, a pencil) and take turns selling it to each other in 30 seconds. Then your kid decides what they'll really sell: something they make, something they own, or a service. They pick something they're proud of and write down why someone would want it, not just what it is.
steps.you: Play the game and be a tough customer: 'Why would I need a spoon?' Then help brainstorm what they could sell, and let them choose. They'll pitch better if it feels like theirs.
ask: In the game, what made you want to buy the spoon?
Who would actually want what you're selling?
steps.tip: The product doesn't need to be perfect. It needs to be something your kid can talk about with real excitement.

levels.explore: Play a few rounds, then pick a product and say one reason someone should buy it.
levels.develop: Pick a product, list 3 reasons it's worth buying, and say who the ideal customer is.
levels.extend: Pick two different customers, like a grandparent and a 10-year-old, and the one reason that sells each.

steps.title: Know the product and the price
steps.why: Your kid gets ready for every question a customer could ask.
steps.kid: Your kid writes down everything about the product: what it's made of, how it's made, what makes it better than the alternatives. Then they turn features into benefits (a feature is what it is; a benefit is what it does for the buyer), work out a price that covers what it cost to make, and prepare answers to the tough questions.
steps.you: Ask tricky customer questions: 'Is it worth the price?' 'Why shouldn't I just make my own?' If they're selling something homemade, help them add up what the ingredients cost, so the price makes a profit.
ask: What does it do for the person who buys it?
If a customer says 'that's too expensive,' what will you say?
steps.tip: Working out the cost per cup or per cookie is the moment the math decides something. Let them do the dividing.

levels.explore: Say 3 great things about it, then pick a price by laying out coins.
levels.develop: List features and benefits separately, set a price that covers your costs, and prepare 3 tough answers.
levels.extend: Split costs into one-time (a sign, a jug) and per item (cups, lemons). How many sales pay back the one-time costs?

steps.title: Write the pitch and practise
steps.why: Your kid writes a 30-second pitch and gets comfortable saying it.
steps.kid: Your kid writes a short pitch like the lemonade example: a hook, the benefit, the price and the ask. They time it at under 30 seconds. Then they practise out loud with a family member playing customer, try different versions, and practise answering questions without reading.
steps.you: Be a realistic practice customer: hesitate, say 'I'm not sure,' ask a question. Then give one specific note: 'Your opening is great, can you make the middle shorter?'
ask: If you only had 10 seconds, what's the one thing you'd say?
What will you do if someone says no?
steps.tip: A pitch in their own words always beats a memorised grown-up script. Help them organise it, but let them find the words.

levels.explore: Say a 3-part pitch on your fingers: hello, why it's great, 'want one?'
levels.develop: Write a hook, benefits and an ask under 30 seconds, and practise with 3 different people.
levels.extend: Write a 10-second and a 30-second version, and practise until you can switch between them without notes.

steps.title: Set up and sell
steps.why: Stall day: a sign, a table, and customers who can say no.
steps.kid: Your kid sets up the stall: a sign that's easy to read from far away, price tags, the product arranged so it looks good. Then they greet each person, give their pitch, answer questions, make change and try to close the sale. They notice which lines work and which fall flat.
steps.you: Help with supplies but let them design the layout. Walk past as if you were a customer: does it catch your eye? Then bring the customers, tell family they're allowed to say no, and step back. Let your kid handle every conversation.
ask: If you saw this stall from across the street, would you walk over?
Did you change your pitch for different people?
steps.tip: Stay close for safety, but out of the conversation. Customers talk to the kid, not the parent standing next to them.

levels.explore: Set up a simple stall with a sign and pitch to 2 or 3 customers.
levels.develop: Add price tags and an eye-catching layout, pitch to 4 or more customers and track which lines worked.
levels.extend: Try two openings on alternate customers and tally which one makes more people stop. Keep the winner.

steps.title: Count it up and look back
steps.why: The numbers, and what your kid learned about persuading people.
steps.kid: Your kid counts the money, subtracts what it cost, and works out the profit. Then they think about the whole experience: what worked, what was hardest, what made people say yes, and what they'd change at the next stall.
steps.you: Celebrate the courage, not just the sales. Standing in front of people and asking them to buy takes guts. Give specific praise: 'You handled that 'too expensive' question really well.'
ask: If you gave a friend one tip about selling, what would it be?
steps.tip: Decide together what happens to the money before stall day: save it, spend it, or split some for the next batch of supplies.

levels.explore: Count the money into piles of $1, then say one thing that went well and one you'd change.
levels.develop: Work out the profit and write a short reflection on what worked in your pitch.
levels.extend: Work out profit per item and profit per hour at the stall. Was it worth the time, and what would raise it?

conclusion.headline: Strangers stopped, listened and paid.
conclusion.text: At the next market or shop counter, watch what they notice. They'll point out a seller's opening line or a sign that caught them, and they can tell you whether it sold a benefit or just named the product.
conclusion.celebrate: The first time someone said no and they pitched the next person anyway, tell them: 'That no didn't slow you down. The next customer got your best pitch.'
extensions: Run a stall at a real community event or market
Add a second product at a different price
Interview a real market vendor about how they sell
Film a 30-second ad for the product

signs: They explain why something is worth it, not just what it is
They bounce back after a 'no' and try a different approach
They start noticing how real shops and stalls catch their eye
makeItReal: Sell at a yard sale, a farmers market kids' table or a community event, with price tags and change to make. Let your kid pick the spot and set up the stall themselves.

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.
